title: Continual Collaborative Distillation for Recommender System

problem.claim: Deploying large-scale recommender systems creates substantial computational burdens, motivating compact models that retain teacher accuracy.

gap.claim: Existing knowledge-distillation studies primarily address one-time distillation in static environments and do not adequately cover continuously changing users, items, and interactions.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes Continual Collaborative Distillation, a framework in which teacher and student models continually and collaboratively evolve along a non-stationary data stream.
The framework helps the student adapt to new data while allowing the teacher to leverage accumulated knowledge.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report extensive quantitative, ablative, and exploratory experiments on two real-world datasets.

narrative_sequence.summary: Knowledge distillation is presented as a way to reduce the computational cost of deploying large-scale recommender systems while retaining accuracy.
Prior work is described as focusing mainly on one-time distillation in static settings, leaving continual data streams insufficiently addressed.
The paper develops a continual, collaborative teacher-student distillation framework for non-stationary data.
The authors report quantitative, ablation, and exploratory experiments on two real-world datasets.
The authors expect the approach to improve the applicability of knowledge distillation in real-world systems.

source_observation.claim: Static, one-time distillation does not directly address continuously arriving users, items, and interactions.

interpretation.claim: Systems deployed on evolving data may require continual adaptation mechanisms rather than a single compression step.

application.claim: For streaming recommender systems, consider updating teacher and student models collaboratively as new data arrives.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether continual collaborative distillation is beneficial outside the reported recommender-system setting.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the two datasets, evaluation metrics, baselines, or numerical results.
The abstract does not specify the teacher and student architectures or the continual update mechanism.
The abstract does not report computational costs, adaptation frequency, or failure cases.
